title: Data Engineering — notebooks, Spark, pipelines, scheduling
description: Intent-scoped fabio skill for Fabric data engineering with code and orchestration: notebooks, Spark (Livy sessions, job definitions), Spark environments/libraries, data pipelines, copy jobs, and job scheduling. Use to author and run transformation code and orchestrate it. Triggers: "notebook", "run notebook", "pyspark", "spark job", "livy", "spark environment", "data pipeline", "copy job", "schedule job", "orchestrate", "etl code".
when_to_use: GET-only environment/Spark triage: environment diagnostics combines explicit configuration/history and selected monitoring session observations, without launching or publishing anything.
Creating/updating notebooks and running them (with parameters, --wait).
Running Spark job definitions or interactive Livy sessions.
Managing Spark environments (libraries, compute settings) and publishing them.
Building and running data pipelines; copy jobs for data movement.
Scheduling recurring runs of notebooks/pipelines/SJDs via the job scheduler.
Orchestrating with Apache Airflow jobs, running dbt (data-build-tool) jobs, or mounting an Azure Data Factory.
when_not_to_use: Loading files/tables into a lakehouse -> use fabio-lakehouse.
Low-code Power Query ETL -> use fabio-dataflows.
T-SQL transformation in a warehouse -> use fabio-warehouse-sql.
CI/CD promotion of these items across environments -> use fabio-deploy-cicd.
must: For a requested live-pool preview, include --dry-run in the command itself; labelling an unguarded submission 'do not execute' is not a dry-run preview. Inspect an already accepted job with --readonly and its exact receipt scope, never by submitting it again.

For explicit Project Osmos requests, explain that the upstream task interface and MWC authentication exist but Fabio has no osmos create/run lifecycle. Direct the user to the reviewed upstream project-osmos skill only with permission to install/execute it; never substitute Fabric data-agent Q&A or Cosmos DB. Read-only listing is not execution approval: separately review the full outcome, resource scope, capacity/cost and write/schema policies. After a task submission timeout preserve task/message IDs, routing and recovery state; inspect the same task read-only, never recreate or replay automatically.
Use --file for notebook source (.py and .ipynb are auto-detected); fabio wraps the format — do NOT hand-build ipynb JSON.
Use --wait/--timeout on notebook/pipeline/SJD runs to observe completion.
Bind a notebook to its default lakehouse with --lakehouse at create time when it reads/writes lakehouse tables.
prefer: Preview release-contract hydration configuration without enabling compute: fabio environment update-staging-spark-compute --workspace <WS> --id <ENV> --compute-api release --custom-live-pool-support Disabled --max-clusters-to-hydrate 1 --cluster-idle-timeout PT20M --custom-live-pool-lifespan PT30M --dry-run. Use --spark-property KEY=VALUE for shape-aware typed merging; raw --file/--content must already match the selected API. Publishing and hydration remain separate approved operations.

Existing live-pool job inspection: fabio job-scheduler get-instance --workspace <WS> --id <ENV> --job-instance-id <JOB> --readonly. New hydration preview with explicitly requested timeout cancellation: fabio environment run-custom-live-pool --workspace <WS> --id <ENV> --wait --timeout <SECONDS> --cancel-on-timeout --dry-run. Omit cancellation unless the user requested it; do not strip dry-run without execution approval.
--file (a written code file) over --content, which is only for small inline snippets.
job-scheduler create-schedule for recurring runs over external cron.
Spark environments to manage libraries once instead of per-notebook installs.
Runtime introspection (context agent --group notebook|spark|data-pipeline) over guessing flags.
avoid: Constructing ipynb JSON manually — pass the file and let fabio handle wrapping.
Assuming a run is done without --wait (async jobs return before completion).
Ignoring cold-start latency on small capacity (first Spark run takes minutes).
key_gotchas: environment run-custom-live-pool now shares receipt-aware job execution: --wait observes only the accepted job, --timeout 1-3600 bounds observation (default 300), and --cancel-on-timeout requires --wait plus explicit approval. Retain jobInstanceId/jobReceipt; receiptPersisted:false, timeout and cancel_requested never authorize replay or prove released capacity. A pool job can run for its configured lifespan, so Completed is not a warm-readiness check. See custom-live-pool-job.

Custom live pools need a custom Spark pool and a published enabled Environment. Explicit --compute-api release selects beta=false and array sparkProperties on get-spark-settings/get-staging-spark-settings/update-staging-spark-compute. Default beta keeps the legacy dictionary contract. Hydration flags require explicit release selection; mismatched raw shapes, duplicate or malformed release properties fail before a PATCH. Typed merging retains unrelated entries/order/unknown fields but is not atomic; coordinate writers. Never silently switch contracts or fall back to starter pools.

Custom live-pool schedule CRUD uses environment jobs/runCustomLivePool/schedules. Keep test schedules disabled; schedule creation does not prove a pool was hydrated. run-custom-live-pool submits compute work and returns its job identity; do not replay an accepted or uncertain submission to obtain status.

Project Osmos is a remote autonomous data-engineering service, not Fabric data-agent Q&A or a Fabio command group. Upstream task/MWC interfaces exist and read-only discovery was verified, but built-in lifecycle mutations are deferred. Route explicit Osmos requests to the reviewed upstream skill only with installation/execution approval; never invent fabio osmos commands, assume the default lakehouse limits scope or recreate a task after uncertainty. See project-osmos.

A cloud connection blocked by DMTS_BlockedByAuthenticationKindPolicies or inter-tenant data-loss-prevention needs tenant-admin allowlist review, not a password reset, workspace grant or identity/credential-mode switch. Do not retry or weaken enforcement automatically. See connection-policies.

environment diagnostics --workspace <WS> --id <ENV> inspects publishing/compute and bounded activation history. Select --activation-id for one resource breakdown; do not assume history is newest-first or Succeeded means clusters are currently warm. Staging differences require review, not automatic publishing.

For session-only triage, environment diagnostics accepts --workspace, --item-type, --item-id and --livy-id without --id; this is the supported session-only invocation, not a missing environment ID. CLI item-type values are lower-case notebook|spark-job-definition|lakehouse, not response enum labels such as Notebook. It reads workspace defaults rather than inventing an environment. Supplying both selections proves no attachment or causality. --include-logs returns metadata only, internally selecting driver stderr and Livy metadata. See spark-diagnostics.

Typed --state on environment list-pool-activations is server-side and conflicts with raw --filter. spark list-livy-sessions --state filters the returned page or --all result, so preserve continuationToken. Monitoring uses NotStarted/InProgress/Succeeded/Failed/Cancelled/Unknown, not interactive Livy idle/busy/dead.

environment show-pool-activation --follow is bounded by --max-duration including in-flight reads. It stops on Succeeded, Failed OR Cancelled; follow_complete reason complete is terminal, not success. Unknown states are not terminal. Follow requires JSON output without --query and never changes activation policy.

Use connection diagnostics --workspace <WS> --item <ITEM> for scoped connection-reference triage. Automatic/SSO references may have no connection ID; PendingOwner is not effective ownership. Caller role/identity metadata is not proof of working source credentials. Do not automatically test credentials, grant roles, or transfer ownership.

Capacity-specific run failures may suggest scoped read-only workspace diagnostics without hidden probes. Those errors do not identify a removable block: diagnose first. Confirmed policy records can yield guarded remediation previews requiring approval, never an automatic run retry or policy change; see remediation-hints.

Watch a running job to completion with 'job-scheduler get-instance --follow': fabio polls the instance on --interval (default 5s), streams NDJSON per cycle, and STOPS EARLY when the status is terminal (Completed/Failed/Cancelled/Deduped) — or when --max-duration / Ctrl-C bounds it (reason 'complete' vs 'max_duration'). Use it to watch an already-running instance (from list-instances or a run-on-demand without --wait); run-on-demand --wait already blocks for jobs you start. Same terminal-aware bounded-follow works on 'operation get-state --follow' (LRO watching: Succeeded/Failed/Canceled/Undefined).
Notebook source cells must be a list of strings in ipynb; fabio builds this for you from --file/--content.
First Spark run on a small capacity is a 2-5 min cold start; LRO may report 430 TooManyRequestsForCapacity when the capacity is saturated.
Environment library changes require a publish (staging/publish) before they take effect.

Fabric Runtime 2.0 (Spark 4.1 / Delta 4.2, Python 3.13) is GA and bare environments in November 2026 validation defaulted to 2.0. Read the selected environment's actual runtime instead of assuming 1.3 or changing it while selecting an API contract. An explicitly approved runtime upgrade can break Python/wheel libraries; review library compatibility and any required republish/removal sequence separately. Delta 4.2 experimental features remain Spark-experience-specific; do not enable them on tables shared across other Fabric workloads automatically.

Environment custom live pools pre-hydrate clusters to reduce cold starts. Explicitly select --compute-api release with --custom-live-pool-support Enabled and hydration flags; the capacity-dependent ceiling is returned as instancePool.maxClustersToHydrateLimit. Disabled retains settings, while --clear-custom-live-pool-settings removes them. Configuring/publishing is not authorization to run hydration.

Environment Spark compute, libraries, and publish have parallel beta/stable API shapes. Compute defaults explicitly to beta=true for compatibility and supports opt-in --compute-api release (beta=false). Other preview-shaped handlers still pin beta=true. The service default switch was postponed to March 31, 2027; never rely on an omitted beta parameter or silently translate payloads.

Spark monitoring uses the validated sparkApplicationId from a selected session. attemptNumber is an observed counter, not a verified URL attempt ID; do not manufacture --attempt-id from it. Without a verified attempt ID the application APIs resolve the service default; diagnostics explicitly marks attemptPinned:false and does not retry guessed attempts. Driver/executor metadata needs --file-name even with --meta (for example stderr); Livy metadata needs neither --app-id nor a file name. Session and environment observations do not prove source authorization or application health.

On-demand job triggers return 202 with the instance id in the Location header (fabio reads it); --wait polls to completion. Copy jobs use their dedicated /copyJobs/{id}/jobs/execute/instances endpoint, honor Retry-After before the first poll, expose copy-job list-runs/show-run, and manage execute schedules with list/create/show/update/delete-schedule. A timeout shorter than Retry-After expires without polling early. Schedule configuration is a complete JSON object with Cron|Daily|Weekly|Monthly type.

environment get-publish-log returns UTF-8 driver stdout for the latest completed publish that ran Spark, whether it succeeded or failed. Inspect contentDisposition/contentType and truncated; the service caps logs at exactly 50,000,000 bytes and appends its truncation marker. No log exists until the Spark-backed publish job completes.

A newly created Copy Job is an empty shell, not a reliable runnable fixture. Lakehouse-to-lakehouse jobs CAN be authored over REST: update copyjob-content.json with properties.source/destination type LakehouseTable, connectionSettings type Lakehouse and typeProperties {workspaceId,artifactId,rootFolder:'Tables'}, plus activities[].properties with source/destination datasetSettings.table, destination writeBehavior:'Append', translator type TabularTranslator, and typeConversionSettings.typeConversion. This shape was live-validated copying real rows; no portal or external connection is required. Verify the persisted activities before running.

Interactive Spark from the CLI uses the INTERACTIVE Livy API (per-lakehouse), which is DISTINCT from the read-only monitoring commands 'spark list-livy-sessions'/'get-livy-session' (workspace-wide, list only). To run code: 'spark run --workspace <WS> --lakehouse <LH> --code "..." --language pyspark|scala|sql|r' is the one-shot primitive (create session -> wait idle -> run -> return output -> ALWAYS delete). Add --high-concurrency (optionally --session-tag <tag>) for a High-Concurrency session: concurrent runs sharing a tag pack onto ONE Spark session (isolated REPLs) — this uses a SEPARATE /highConcurrencySessions endpoint, NOT a Spark --conf. For multiple statements on one warm session use 'spark create-livy-session --wait' + 'spark run-statement --session-id' + 'spark delete-livy-session'. Async statement control: 'spark submit-statement' returns immediately with a statementId, 'spark get-statement' polls it, and 'spark cancel-statement' STOPS it — important because 'run-statement --timeout' only bounds the WAIT; the statement keeps RUNNING and consuming Spark capacity after a timeout until you cancel it. Gotchas: a cold session takes ~100s to reach 'idle' (--timeout defaults to 300s); Spark SQL results are NOT text/plain — they come back under data['application/json'] as {schema, data:[[...]]}, while pyspark/scala print output is in 'text'; a session created with create-livy-session keeps consuming capacity until delete-livy-session (the one-shot 'run' self-cleans).

troubleshooting.symptom: Notebook run returns before the work is done
troubleshooting.fix: Add --wait --timeout <secs>; the run is async (202 + polling).
Capacity is saturated; retry later, reduce concurrency, or use a larger capacity.

troubleshooting.symptom: Notebook can't find its lakehouse tables
troubleshooting.fix: Create it with --lakehouse $LH so the default lakehouse (trident) metadata is injected.

troubleshooting.symptom: Installed library not available at runtime
troubleshooting.fix: Publish the Spark environment (environment staging/publish) and attach it to the notebook.

safety: Diagnostics/follow do not start work, publish/cancel, or change pools. Historical failure, partial evidence, staging differences and empty advice never authorize a restart, publish, pool change or source probe.
Deleting a notebook/pipeline/SJD removes its definition — confirm with the user.
Scheduling a recurring job commits ongoing capacity consumption — confirm cadence and timezone.
